sections.h: Atrahasis: six years of famine sent by the gods
sections.b: In the Babylonian poem Atrahasis, the god Enlil, kept awake by humanity's noise, locks the sky, the deep and the sea so that no food can reach the people (Atrahasis 7:68-79). The famine is told year by year: the old grain eaten, the storehouse opened, faces darkened, bodies shrunk, mothers and daughters sold for silver, and in the sixth year children eaten (Atrahasis 8:77-95). The Bible tells of the same horrors in sieges (2 Kings 6:28-29; Lamentations 4:10) and as the last curse of a broken covenant (Leviticus 26:29). The difference is the reason. In the poem the gods starve people to make them quiet. In the Bible famine comes as a warning against real evil, meant to bring people back (Amos 4:6-9), and God is the one who feeds (Psalm 145:15-16).

sections.b: Against an earlier drought, the god Enki tells Atrahasis to have the people stop worshiping every god but Adad, the storm god, and to shame him with gifts of bread and flour until he sends dew and mist (Atrahasis 7:9-58). The Bible names one Giver of rain, who cannot be bribed (Deuteronomy 10:17; Jeremiah 14:22) and who gives rain even to the ungrateful (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17).

common: Ancient peoples on every side of Israel saw drought and famine as the anger of the gods.
uncommon: Some readers see Atrahasis' plague, drought and famine as a parallel to the 120 years of grace in Genesis 6:3 before the Flood (mentioned by A. R. Millard).

sections.h: Atrahasis: the oath of the flood
sections.b: In Atrahasis, after the god Enki ends the famine by letting the fish of the sea loose, Enlil calls the whole assembly of the gods to swear to the flood, and they swear, Anu first (Atrahasis 9:77-80). Enki refuses to be bound: "Should I bring my hand down on my own people?" (Atrahasis 9:141). Tablet II ends: "Enlil has done an evil work against the people" (Atrahasis 9:168). The Bible turns the oath around. God swears after the Flood that it will never happen again (Isaiah 54:9; Genesis 9:11), and in Genesis the one who sends the Flood is the same God who warns and saves Noah (Genesis 6:17-18).

claude.title: Whose evil?
claude.body: My reading: the most important difference between Atrahasis and Genesis is where the evil lies. The poem says plainly that its high god did evil to the people (Atrahasis 9:168), and the people were guilty only of being many and loud. Genesis says the evil was in the human heart (Genesis 6:5) and that the Judge of all the earth does what is just (Genesis 18:25). A flood story told by people who did not know the just God would have to blame the gods; Genesis tells it from the side of the one who knows.

sections.h: Atrahasis: a council with no judge above it
sections.b: In Tablet II of Atrahasis the gods rule by assembly and oath. Enlil calls them together again and again (Atrahasis 7:68), charges Enki before them (Atrahasis 9:14-37), and makes them all swear to the flood (Atrahasis 9:77-80). Enki is accused, defends himself, and refuses to be put under oath (Atrahasis 9:140). Psalm 82 also pictures a council of "gods", but God stands in it as Judge and condemns them for injustice (Psalm 82:1-8). The Babylonian council has no one over it, and its ruling is admitted to be evil (Atrahasis 9:168).

sections.h: Atrahasis: worship one god, as a tactic
sections.b: Enki's advice against the drought sounds like the first commandment: "'Do not revere your gods; / do not pray to your goddess" (Atrahasis 7:17-18), but seek Adad alone. It is a tactic, not a confession: the people are to shame the rain god with bread (Atrahasis 7:20-38). Elijah's demand at Carmel, "If the LORD is the God, go after him" (1 Kings 18:21), asks who is real, not who can be bought, and Hosea accuses Israel of thanking Baal for grain the LORD gave (Hosea 2:8).

sections.h: Atrahasis: the broken bolt of the sea
sections.b: In Atrahasis the god Enki guards "the bolt and rope that lock in the sea" with his hairy servants (Atrahasis 7:74-79). The famine ends when the sea's two gatekeepers break the bolt and the fish escape to feed the people (Atrahasis 9:118-122), and Enki is blamed for losing control. A. R. Millard noted that the sea here is not the dragon Tiamat but an unruly element that must be held in, and compared the Bible's passages on God shutting in the sea (Job 38:8-11; Psalm 104:9). In the Bible the sea never breaks loose from its Maker (Mark 4:39-41).

sections.h: Atrahasis: a prayer sent down the river
sections.b: In Atrahasis the hero weeps day after day, brings incense, makes an offering at midnight and asks the river to carry his gift to his god Enki, praying for a dream (Atrahasis 8:6-26). Messengers come back across the sea, and he asks how his prayer got through (Atrahasis 8:45). The scene is close to Daniel's mourning by the Tigris, answered by a heavenly messenger: "your words were heard" (Daniel 10:12). But the Bible's God needs no courier: "Your Father knows the things you have need of before you ever ask him" (Matthew 6:8).

sections.h: Atrahasis: asking a god for a dream
sections.b: Atrahasis offers incense and a sacrifice, sleeps by the river and asks his god for a dream (Atrahasis 8:9-26). Mesopotamians sought messages from their gods in this way. The Bible tells of God speaking in dreams after sacrifice, as to Solomon at Gibeon (1 Kings 3:4-5), but there the dream is God's free gift, not something a worshiper can secure.

In Tablet II of Atrahasis the gods bind themselves by oath to Enlil's plans (Atrahasis 7:12; 9:15), swear to the flood (Atrahasis 9:78-80), and try to put Enki under oath; he refuses (Atrahasis 9:136-141). The Bible's great oath runs the other way: God swears by himself to bless and to spare (Hebrews 6:13; Isaiah 54:9).

sections.b: The god Enki sends his lahmu, long-haired beings of his waters, across the sea to the weeping Atrahasis, and he bows and kisses the ground before them (Atrahasis 8:32-55). The pattern of a messenger sent to one who prays is shared with the Bible (Daniel 10:12; Hebrews 1:14), but the Bible's angels refuse worship: "Do not do it! ... Worship God!" (Revelation 22:9).

One Old Babylonian copy of Atrahasis says that when Enki heard of the famine, "his tears ran down in pity" (Atrahasis 8:100-102). He weeps, but he is one god outvoted by others and can act only by tricks. Genesis says the LORD "was sorry that he had made humankind on the earth, and it pained him to his heart" (Genesis 6:6); the one who grieves is also the one who judges and saves.

sections.h: Atrahasis Tablet II and the Bible's droughts
sections.b: Tablet II of Atrahasis (Atrahasis 6-9) tells of drought and famine sent by the god Enlil to silence humanity, ended each time by the god Enki, until the gods swear to the flood. Its pictures are close to the Bible's: a sky shut up and the springs of the deep held back (Atrahasis 8:69-71; Genesis 8:2), salt in the fields (Psalm 107:34), children sold and eaten in famine (Nehemiah 5:5; Lamentations 4:10). A. R. Millard noted that the scheme of crises before the Flood has no counterpart in Genesis, while the idea of human provocation leading to the Flood is common to both.
